extraction.name: The LAMBADA dataset
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages such that human subjects are able to guess the last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, German Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernandez
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, Denis; Kruszewski, German; Lazaridou, Angeliki; Pham, Quan Ngoc; Bernardi, Raffaella; Pezzelle, Sandro; Baroni, Marco; Boleda, Gemma; Fernandez, Raquel. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context and a target sentence, where the task is to guess the last word of the target sentence. The data come from the Book Corpus of unpublished novels. The corpus was divided into training and development+testing partitions by novel. To reduce time and cost, passages that were relatively easy for standard language models were filtered out automatically. A random sample of the remaining passages was then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: one subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; if correct, a second subject guessed from the whole passage; if also correct, additional subjects guessed from the target sentence only until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. If no subject could guess the target word from the sentence alone, the passage was added to the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data come from the Book Corpus, containing unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The corpus was randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions by novel. Duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list were applied to the Book Corpus. Passages whose target word had probability greater than or equal to 0.00175 according to any of four language models were excluded. The same novel-based division method was used to further split LAMBADA data between development and testing.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each passage was constructed with a context size defined as the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. The target word was constrained to be the last word of the target sentence. The Book Corpus was preprocessed by duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Automated filtering removed passages easy for standard language models before human evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotation was conducted through CrowdFlower in three steps. First, one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage. If correct, a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage. If also correct, more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10. Subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. Passages were included only if two consecutive subjects exactly matched the missing word using the whole passage and no subject out of ten could provide it from the local sentence context alone.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Step 2 was added based on a pilot study showing that step 1 alone did not ensure that the data were easy given the discourse context. The authors made sure that the same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions. They adopted a strict hit-or-miss approach requiring exact matches, rather than allowing plausible or synonymous continuations, because determining acceptable alternatives would be practically and methodologically challenging. In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2, and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 12 human judgments for included items: 1 in step 1, 1 in step 2, and up to 10 unsuccessful sentence-only judgments in step 3.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A pre-trained recurrent neural network and three models trained on the Book Corpus: a standard 4-gram model, a recurrent neural network, and a feed-forward model.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded from the project website. The test set will be made available at the time of the competition. The paper states plans to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is proposed as a challenging benchmark meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%), with verbs, adjectives, and adverbs being rare. Proper nouns are hugely overrepresented compared to the input distribution. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. The items also contain quoted direct speech more often than the input items overall (71% vs. 61%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was constructed with very strict inclusion criteria requiring exact word matches by two broad-context subjects and failure by sentence-only subjects, which excludes plausible or synonymous continuations. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality. The authors note that standard language models are bound to fail on LAMBADA by design because one of the first filters selected passages where simple language models failed to predict the upcoming word. The training data are from the same domain as the development and test passages but are not filtered in the same way.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a challenging test set and benchmark for evaluating computational models on their ability to use broad discourse context in word prediction and natural language understanding. The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages. Models tackling LAMBADA should be trained on raw text from the training partition composed of 2,662 novels and more than 200 million words.
